judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 10, which would have added a 12th seat to the University of Alaska Board of Regents. The new seat would have gone to a full-time professor with tenure. Each of the three campus faculty senates would have picked two names. The governor would have chosen one of the six for a two-year term. The legislature would have had to approve the choice. The number of regents needed to do business would have risen from six to seven. The extra seat would have ended in February 2033. The Alaska House accepted the Senate's changes 26-14. The governor vetoed the bill, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 133, which would have given the state a deadline to pay its bills. An agency would have had 45 days to pay a contractor after a proper request. That would have dropped to 30 days later on. After the deadline the agency would have owed interest. The same rule would have covered grants owed to nonprofits, cities, boroughs and Alaska Native groups. An agency holding back a payment would have had eight working days to explain why in writing. The Alaska House accepted the Senate's changes 22-18. The governor vetoed the bill, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 25, which would have stopped restaurants from serving food in polystyrene foam containers. That is the white plastic foam often called Styrofoam. The state could not have bought it either. Food packed outside Alaska would not have been covered. Neither would an area under a disaster emergency. A restaurant could have asked the state for an exemption if the cost was too hard to bear. A city or borough could also have opted out for its own restaurants. The Alaska House accepted the Senate's changes 26-14. The governor vetoed the bill, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 26, which would have told the state to write a transit plan for the whole of Alaska. Transit means buses, vans and other shared rides. The plan would have covered public, tribal and community transit. The transportation department would have built it with local governments, tribes and transit groups. Ferry operators and the Alaska Railroad would also have taken part. The bill added these kinds of transit to the department's standing duties. The Alaska House accepted the Senate's changes 22-14. The governor vetoed the bill, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 280, which would have changed how Alaska taxes the profit of a company that works in many states. Alaska now looks at where the company does its work. The bill would have looked at where the customer is instead. A sale of a service or a digital product would have counted as an Alaska sale when the buyer is here. Television and cable programmers would have used the customer's home base. Phone and internet companies would have kept the current test. The Alaska House accepted the Senate's changes 28-11. The governor vetoed the bill, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 52, which would have set new rules for children staying in psychiatric hospitals. A child could have had two hours a week of private phone or video contact with a parent. A court or the doctor in charge could have blocked it. Hospitals would have had to report each time they held a child alone or used a restraint. The report would have gone to the state and the parent within 72 hours. The state would have checked these hospitals twice a year without warning. Inspectors would have talked to at least half the children with staff out of the room. The Alaska House accepted the Senate's changes 26-14. The governor vetoed the bill. The legislature fell short of the votes to override, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 69, which would have raised the base student allocation from $5,960 to $6,960. That number is the dollar amount per student in Alaska's school funding formula. Raising it would have sent more state money to every school district. The change would have started in July 2025. The Alaska House accepted the Senate's changes 21-16. The governor vetoed the bill. The legislature fell short of the votes to override, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 113, which would have changed how Alaska taxes the profit of a company that works in many states. Alaska now looks at where the company does its work. The bill would have looked at where the customer is instead. A sale of a service or a digital product would have counted as an Alaska sale when the buyer is here. Some companies earn at least half their Alaska sales online or by electronic delivery. Those companies would have been taxed on their sales here alone. Today the tax also weighs their property and payroll. The Alaska House passed it 26-14. The governor vetoed the bill. The legislature fell short of the votes to override, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 21, which would have created a state savings plan for retirement called Alaska Work and Save. It would have covered an employer that had employed more than five people in Alaska for at least three years and offered no retirement plan. That employer would have had to send part of each worker's pay into a state-run account. Workers would have joined automatically at a set rate that rises over time. They could have opted out or changed the rate at any time. The state would have invested the money but promised no return. Workers could also have put their permanent fund dividend into the account. The Alaska House passed it 31-9. The governor vetoed the bill. The legislature fell short of the votes to override, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 24, which would have raised the legal age for buying or having tobacco, nicotine and vaping products. The age would have gone from 19 to 21. Workers aged 19 and 20 could still have sold them at work. The bill would have taxed throwaway vapes at 25 percent of the shop price. Lab-made nicotine would have fallen under the existing wholesale tobacco tax. The vape money would have gone to a state program that helps people quit. The bill also set new rules for shipping these products into Alaska. It would have let people smoke cigars inside stores that mostly sell cigars. The Alaska House passed it 24-16. The governor vetoed the bill, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 258, which would have barred state software contracts from limiting which computers the state may use. The rule would have covered software built for ordinary desktop or server machines. The state could still have agreed to a limit needed for a federal rule or a security rule. It could also have agreed to one built into the way the software works. It could still have bought a cheaper bundle with a limit, if it put the reason in writing. The Alaska House passed it 26-13. The governor vetoed the bill, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 41, which would have added mental health to the health lessons Alaska schools are urged to teach. The lessons run from kindergarten through grade 12. The state board of education would have written guidelines for them. The guidelines would have used content based on medicine and science. They could not have carried political or advocacy material unrelated to student mental health. Schools would have had to tell parents two weeks before any class on mental health. A parent could have pulled a child out. The Alaska House passed it 27-13. The governor vetoed the bill. The legislature fell short of the votes to override, so it did not become law.
